opus-5.5.text:
I think the value is really in the long tail of use cases that a general model will never cover perfectly out of the box. When we release a speech model, it's trained to be good across a broad range of languages, accents, and acoustic conditions. But the moment you go into a real deployment, you hit very specific things: a call center with a particular kind of background noise, a hospital where people use a lot of medical terminology and drug names, a company with internal product names and acronyms that no public dataset will ever contain. A base model will get most of the transcript right, but it's exactly those rare, domain-specific words that matter most to the customer, and those are the ones it tends to miss.

Fine-tuning lets people close that gap with relatively little data. You don't need millions of hours; often a few hours of in-domain audio with good transcripts makes a big difference on word error rate for the terms people actually care about. And it's not only vocabulary. Accents and dialects are a big one. There are many languages and regional variants that are underrepresented in training data, and the people who have the best data for those are often local companies, universities, or communities. Giving them the ability to adapt the model is much more effective than us trying to collect everything centrally.

There's also the deployment side. A lot of our customers want to run models on their own infrastructure, sometimes on-prem, for privacy reasons, especially with voice data, which is very sensitive. If they can fine-tune on their own data without that data ever leaving their environment, that unlocks use cases that would otherwise be impossible.

And more broadly, it's consistent with how we've always thought about models: we want to give people open weights and the tools to customize them, because the community ends up building things we would never have anticipated. With text models, we saw people fine-tune for coding, for specific languages, for very niche tasks, and a lot of the most interesting applications came from that. I expect the same thing with speech. The base model is a starting point; the real value gets created when people adapt it to their own problems.

r001.rationale: It says fine-tuning can adapt the model to underrepresented languages and regional variants using data from local companies, universities, or communities.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting the model to domain-specific needs such as medical terminology, internal product names, and call-center conditions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't know all the use cases, and that's exactly why fine-tuning matters. When we release a model like Voxtral, we have a certain picture of what people want: transcription, maybe some speech understanding, a few languages. But the moment it goes out, people come back with things we never considered. A hospital wants it to understand medical vocabulary with a specific accent. A call center in Brazil wants Portuguese with a lot of domain-specific jargon. Someone wants a model that handles code-switching between French and Arabic in the same sentence. We can't train for all of that centrally.

There's also a data question. The data that matters most for these niche cases is often data we don't have and shouldn't have. It's private, it's proprietary, it's sitting inside a company. Fine-tuning lets people bring the model to their data instead of sending their data to us. That's especially important in speech, because audio is very personal. You can hear who someone is.

And from a research side, I find it genuinely interesting. Speech models are much less explored than text models in terms of what fine-tuning can do. With text, the community has spent years figuring out LoRA, instruction tuning, all of that. With audio, people are still discovering how much you can shift a model with a few hours of data, how to handle low-resource languages, where the model breaks. Opening that up means thousands of people experimenting instead of a small team at Mistral. We learn from that too.

So the value is partly practical, you get models that actually work for your case, and partly that it's the fastest way to find out what these models are capable of.

r001.rationale: It identifies fine-tuning for handling low-resource languages, a clear equivalent of extending support to tail languages.

r002.rationale: It gives adapting the model to domain-specific jargon in Portuguese and medical vocabulary as use cases.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is in adapting the model to use cases that we can’t anticipate. With speech, you have different languages, accents, recording conditions, and specialized vocabulary. If you’re transcribing a conversation in a particular industry, getting those technical terms right can make a huge difference.

Fine-tuning gives people a way to use their own examples to improve the model for that setting. And for speech generation, you may want a particular voice or speaking style. So instead of relying on one model to serve everyone equally well, people can adapt it to what they actually need.

r001.rationale: The response mentions adapting to different languages, but does not identify fine-tuning as a way to extend support to tail or less common languages.

r002.rationale: It describes improving transcription of technical terms for a particular industry, clearly identifying adaptation to a specialized domain within a language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is in letting people adapt the model to their particular use case. Speech has so much variation: accents, languages, specialized vocabulary, the way people speak in a particular environment. You can build a very good general model, but you’re never going to cover every situation equally well.

If someone has data from their own application, fine-tuning gives them a way to improve the things that matter to them without having to train a model from scratch. And people will find applications that we wouldn’t necessarily think of ourselves. That’s a big part of the value of putting these models in developers’ hands.

r001.rationale: The response mentions adapting to different languages, but does not identify tail languages as a use case.

r002.rationale: It mentions specialized vocabulary and application-specific data, but does not clearly identify adapting to a specialized domain within an existing language.
